nodes.question: Which studies are referenced regarding the investigation of imperfectly competitive environmental industries?
nodes.answer: The studies referenced for investigating imperfectly competitive environmental industries include works by David and Sinclair-Desgagn (2005, 2010) and Canton (2007).
nodes.paragraph: The environmental goods sector has grown more rapidly than the overall economy of countries. For example, in the European Union, * Mutsumi Matsumoto matsumoto.mutsumi.n5@f.mail.nagoya-u.ac.jp; mmt06834@ec.ritsumei.ac.jp 1 Graduate School of Environmental Studies, Nagoya University, Furo-Cho, Chikusa-Ku, Nagoya 464-8601, Japan 2 Ritsumeikan University, Nishinokyo-Suzaku 1, Nakagyo-Ku, Kyoto 604-8520, Japan Environmental Economics and Policy Studies the average annual growth rate of gross value added in this sector was 3.4% from 2000 to 2020, whereas the GDP grew by 1.0% on average per year. 1 In the United States, from 2000 to 2022, with the exception of 2015, the annual revenue growth rate of environmental industries was higher than the GDP growth rate.2 Given the heightened awareness of environmental and social governance, this trend is expected to continue. Markets for environmental goods tend to be highly segmented and imperfectly competitive because pollution abatement technologies are usually protected by pat- ents (Sinclair-Desgagn , 2011, 2017).3 In the literature on environmental policies and pollution abatement, the case of imperfectly competitive environmental indus- tries has been investigated by David and Sinclair-Desgagn (2005, 2010), Canton (2007), Canton et al.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Industry, innovation and infrastructure|Sustainable industry|Industrial ecology_qna_001
nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: Why is it important to address environmental challenges in an interconnected manner?
nodes.answer: Addressing environmental challenges in an interconnected manner is important to avoid inefficiencies and missed opportunities, as integrative solutions can bring co-benefits and synergetic outcomes for different sectors.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Environmental challenges are increasingly often interconnected. Yet, they are commonly addressed separately, which might result in inef ciencies and missed opportunities. While it is widely acknowledged that integrative solutions can bring co- bene its and synergetic outcomes for different sectors, empirical studies that systematically explore cross-sector integration at the operational level are rare. Drawing from two case studies with a high potential for reducing the environmental impacts of energy production and agriculture while restoring nature in the Dutch rural context, this exploratory study aims to provide an improved understanding of the institutional factors that in uence the ful Ilment of integrative potential in rural areas. To understand how institutional factors in uence integrative outcomes, we use the operational level rules that guide actions and interactions among the actors of the Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework. Our analysis shows that the potential of integrative solutions is not fully recognized and realized in Dutch rural areas. Key institutional factors thathamper integration are diverging perceptions of desired outcomes (scope rule), exclusion of important actors from decision- making (position rule), and imbalances in the sharing of costs and bene its (payoff rule).

nodes.question: How has industrial development impacted natural resources according to the paragraph?
nodes.answer: Industrial development has led to increased exploitation of natural resources, which has been observed to generate revenue but also causes environmental pollution.
nodes.paragraph: Such inclusion may guide policymakers to suggest eco-friendly suggestions for a green environment. Secondly , social factors such as urbanization are important environmental determinants that cannot be excluded from the development models. For instance, its immense demand for society S development and interconnected sectors may bring environmental pollution via the usage of energy-intensive products. Rapid urbanization would cause environmental stress at the domestic level, but this connection has not yet been answered clearly, and practitioners are curious to know the actual situation in WRE economies. To answer this question, the current study and its outcomes may guide policymakers to take green urbanization initiatives. Thirdly , the depletion of natural resources (NRs) has remained a rich source of revenue for earning and investing in development plans. The exploitation of NRs has recently been observed due to industrial development plans. The selected economies also believed in globalization, exporting goods & services, and extracting available natural resources for trade activities that further cause environmental deterioration. The current theme also considers natural resource exploitation as an environmental determinant to answer whether it raises domestic environmental pollution.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Industry, innovation and infrastructure|Sustainable industry|Industrial ecology_qna_004
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What overarching theory is used to explore the issue of sustainable waste management in this context?
nodes.answer: The overarching theory used to explore the issue of sustainable waste management is social ecology theory, which explains the relationship between nature and society.
nodes.paragraph: Addressing sustainable solid waste management (SWM) can help meet several United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDG), such as, creating sustainable cities and inclusive communities (SDG11)1 and ensuring sustainable consumption and production patterns (SDG 12).2 Recent studies indicate that the waste sectors in develop- ing countries remain heavily focused on waste collection and removal rather than a holistic waste management approach (Nguyen et al. 2023, p. 1; Wilson 2007, p. 202). Teshome (2021, p. 18) summarized the waste management systems in developing countries as exhibiting 3ls irregular, inad- equate, and inefficient. If sustainable waste management is not prioritized, the balance between nature and society threaten to collapse due to toxins from waste pollution, loss of biodiversity and adverse impacts of climate change. Con- sequently, the drive to achieve SDG 11 and SDG 12 would not be met. Hence the need to find sustainable waste man - agement practices is critical in many developing nations like Botswana. To explore this issue, we use social ecology theory as the overarching theory to explain the relationship between nature and society.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Industry, innovation and infrastructure|Sustainable industry|Industrial ecology_qna_005
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What theory is discussed in relation to waste management studies in sub-Saharan Africa?
nodes.answer: Social ecology theory is discussed in relation to waste management studies in sub-Saharan Africa.
nodes.paragraph: 2013, p. 7 of 20; Blanco 2011; Budiharta et al. 2016; Ostrom 2009). All these studies suggest that local communities involvement is crucial in the sustainable management of resources. Social ecology theory has also been used in waste management studies and local knowledge in sub-Saharan Africa (Muheirwe et al. 2023, p. 1; Anokye & Mohammed 2024). Both studies highlight the importance of local knowl- edge to sustainable waste management strategies and criti- cize the apparent disregard for local knowledge as a viable alternative solution. On the other hand studies on Botswana communities using the social ecology theory have been limited to wildlife management (Blackie and Sowa 2019 ; Mbaiwa 2015; Mbaiwa and Hambira 2023). While the social ecology theory has been successfully applied to wildlife management and Community-Based Natural Resource Management (CBNRM) in Botswana, the use of the SES framework in waste management studies is still rare. Despite government efforts to regulate waste management through legislation, many households continue to use harmful practices like burning, burying, or dumping waste. To address these gaps, this study aims to explore the role of local knowledge as a solution for enhancing waste management in Borakalalo ward in Molepolole, Botswana.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Industry, innovation and infrastructure|Sustainable industry|Industrial ecology_qna_007
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What does the paper argue about the relationship between industrial societies' natural resource use and ecological regeneration processes?
nodes.answer: The paper argues that the current use of natural resources by industrialized societies is incompatible with the regeneration processes of ecological systems.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract In this paper, we show that the characteristics of complex adaptive systems support the original interpretation of the bioeconomy of Georgescu-Roegen: the current use of natural resources by industrialized societies is incompatible with the regeneration processes of ecological systems. Elaborating the concept of societal identity, using a biosemiotics reading of the social theory of Luhmann, we show that the current social identity is sustained by implausible sociotechnical imaginaries, including the European Union S interpretation of the bioeconomy as a panacea for green growth. We argue that the current widespread perception of polycrisis is a sign that, on the tangible side of biosemiotic process, social practices urgently need change. On the notional side, however, society is (still) incapable of relinquishing the set of sociotechnical imaginaries grounded in the American and Cartesian dreams (the promethean ideology) firmly locked in its collective memory. This incongruity has produced information disorder in the sustainability discourse. We conclude that the EU endorsement of the concept of the circular (bio)economy as a strategy for perpetual economic growth decoupled from resource use represents a desperate attempt to maintain the status quo through the endorsement of an integrated set of noble lies.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Industry, innovation and infrastructure|Sustainable industry|Industrial ecology_qna_008
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: Which analysis developed by the Odum brothers is referenced in the context of ecosystem structure?
nodes.answer: eMergy analysis is referenced as an approach to studying the functional structure of ecosystems developed by the Odum brothers.
nodes.paragraph: In this section, we present a completely different approach grounded in the fields of chemistry and ecology to provide further theoretical support for the incompatibility of the pattern of economic growth of contemporary society with ecological processes. More specifically, we set out why the metabolic identity of post-industrial society is incompatible with that of natural ecosystems. Key to our argument is the concept of group autocatalysis or collectively autocatalytic set first introduced by Kauffman, who used the concept to explain the origin of life (Hordijk 2019; Kauffman 1993). [A similar concept is the hypercycle, originally introduced in chemistry, which refers to a special form of organization emerging in chemical reactions (Eigen 1971; Eigen and Schuster 1977, 1978)]. The concept has been applied in theoretical ecology to study the mechanisms of formation of structural and functional relations in complex adaptive systems. Examples are eMergy analysis of the functional structure of ecosystems developed by the Odum brothers (Odum 1971a, b), ascendency analysis developed and used by Ulanowicz (1986, 1997) to study the difference between growth and development in ecosystems, and metabolism repair relational network proposed by Rosen (1958, 1959, 1977, 1978, 1985, 2005, 2012) and further developed by Louie (2009, 2013, 2017).
